cards.title: Gate a free sample so it reads as a gift, not a trial
cards.summary: Frame samples and freebies as gifts (unrequested, non-returnable) to trigger the reciprocity rule and lift purchase or donation conversion.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to add a free sample, gift-with-purchase, or unsolicited freebie to a PDP, cart, sampling program, or acquisition offer.
steps: Recognize that a small free sample works on two levels: it lets the customer try the product, and it functions as a gift that creates a sense of obligation to reciprocate. Cialdini notes the promoter 'can release the natural indebting force inherent in a gift while innocently appearing to have only the intention to inform.'

Make the gift genuinely unrequested and framed as a gift the customer keeps ('it's our gift to you'), not as a paid or trial unit. Reciprocity fires even on unwanted gifts: the Hare Krishna solicitors pressed flowers on passersby, refused to take them back, then asked for a donation — donors often gave a dollar or two and then threw the flower away.
Do not require the customer to opt in or return the item. The obligation to receive is described as the exploitable part of the rule: it lets the giver choose who becomes indebted.

For ecommerce, test unrequested free inserts (sample sachet, extra unit, printed insert gift, free shipping on a first order) placed before the purchase ask, and measure purchase conversion against a no-gift control.
Track whether recipients actually value the gift; the Krishna flower worked even though a large share were discarded, but for a store a worthless gift risks brand damage and a wasted sample budget.
caveats: Reciprocity is a nudge, not a guarantee; the effect weakens when recipients recognize the tactic as a ploy.
Airports eventually posted warnings about the Krishna solicitors and travelers learned to avoid them, showing public awareness can neutralize the tactic.
Deliberately creating obligation can backfire on brand trust if customers feel cornered.

cards.title: Free-sample tactics: self-serve cutting and leave-behind kits
cards.summary: Two formats of sampling — self-serve cut portions and home leave-behind kits — that let customers try before buying and generate orders.
cards.use_when: Designing an in-store or at-home sampling program, or adapting samples to a subscription or replenishment offer.
steps: Self-serve format: Cialdini cites an Indiana supermarket operator who sold roughly 1,000 pounds of cheese in a few hours by putting out the cheese and inviting customers to cut their own free slivers. Applying this to a store, the suggested adaptation is a free sample station or a free mini-size of a consumable, since the customer's own small action creates purchase momentum.

Leave-behind format: Amway's BUG was a tray or bag of household products (polish, detergent, shampoo, deodorizer, insect killer, window cleaner) left with a household for 24, 48, or 72 hours at no cost or obligation, then collected and moved to the next prospect.
Refill logistics: because customers rarely empty the containers in that period, leftover product can be rotated to the next household; some representatives ran several BUGs at once.
Amway reported customers bought about half the total BUG contents on average, per distributor reports in the source. Treat as a company-reported case, not a benchmark.

For ecommerce, the transferable move is a free or low-cost trial of a consumable, a starter kit, or a sample box with no obligation, followed by a purchase ask after the trial window — not a free trial that demands data or a subscription up front.
caveats: Amway figures are distributor-reported anecdotes from the source, not verified rates any store should expect.
Leave-behind kits only work with reusable or partially consumed product and a repeat pick-up touchpoint; most ecommerce stores must replicate this with shipping, which changes the economics.

cards.title: Uninvited gifts create debt even when unwanted
cards.summary: Unrequested gifts, even ones the recipient dislikes or discards, trigger repayment pressure that raises response rates.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to add unsolicited inserts, samples, or gifts to an acquisition mailing, unboxing, or retargeting campaign.
steps: Use the Disabled American Veterans figures as the reference case: a plain mail appeal produced about 18% response; adding an unsolicited gift (gummed, individualized address labels) nearly doubled it to 35%.
Note the mechanism: the rule only requires repayment of what was given, so an unrequested gift still creates obligation — a requested favor is not needed to produce debt.

Apply this to ecommerce by including an unrequested physical or digital gift in the first touch (insert in the box, a free guide, address labels, a small sample) and frame accompanying copy as 'a gift' rather than a purchased item. The source notes gifts avoid the cultural pressure attached to buying an unwanted commercial product, so gift framing can outperform a straight discount.
If you use the gift to ask for something — a review, a referral, a repeat purchase, an email signup — time the ask after delivery of the gift.
Measure with a control group: compare the response rate with and without the unrequested gift, since results depend on the audience and the gift's perceived fit.
caveats: Reciprocity is weaker for gifts recipients are indifferent to or that feel like a trick; the effect is cultural and not a mechanical guarantee.
The 18%/35% figures come from one organization's mailing; do not treat them as a prediction for any store.

cards.title: Use rejection-then-retreat to make a smaller ask land
cards.summary: Make a large request first and retreat to the request you actually want; the retreat is read as a concession to reciprocate.
cards.use_when: Structuring an offer ladder, upsell, price negotiation, referral ask, or checkout offer so the real target request is framed as a concession.
steps: Ask for the larger item or commitment first, let the customer decline, then present the request you wanted all along. Cialdini's Boy Scout case: he asked $5 circus tickets, was refused, then offered $1 chocolate bars and got a sale.

The second request doesn't have to be small in absolute terms — it only has to be smaller than the first. In Cialdini's zoo experiment, students first asked for a 2-year, 2-hour-per-week counseling commitment (all refused), then asked to chaperone a one-day zoo trip; compliance tripled, from 17% to 50%.

Make the initial request plausible enough to be seen as good-faith bargaining. Bar-Ilan research cited in the source shows that a first demand so extreme it looks unreasonable backfires, because the later retreat is not read as a genuine concession.

For ecommerce: open a pricing or bundle conversation with the premium tier or largest bundle, then retreat to the mid-tier you intended to sell; or ask for a large commitment (annual plan, full-size) before dropping to the smaller commit you want.

Apply it to referral asks too: after a purchase refusal or declined offer, ask for names of friends who might be interested, framed as a retreat from the purchase request. The source describes door-to-door trainers using exactly this sequence.
caveats: Works only if the retreat looks like a real concession; a contrived or absurd first ask is detected and refused.
Strongest as a negotiation and offer-structuring technique; using it as a dark pattern at checkout can damage repeat trust.

cards.title: Perceptual contrast: show the expensive anchor first
cards.summary: Presenting a high-priced item before a lower one makes the lower price feel smaller, lifting the lower-priced sale — and sometimes the average sale.
cards.use_when: Ordering products on a pricing page, bundle ladder, PDP comparison, or in-store/assisted selling sequence.
steps: Expose the buyer to the larger price first. Just as a sweater seems cheap after a suit purchase, the smaller request looks smaller when preceded by a larger one.

Cialdini cites Brunswick billiard tables: a store's first week showed customers the low end and traded them up, producing a $550 average sale; the second week led all customers to a $3,000 table first and then let them shop down the line by price and quality, producing over $1,000 average. Treat this as the source's store-reported example, not a general benchmark.
This is the retail practice of 'talking the top of the line': if the customer buys the deluxe model, great; if not, counteroffer with a more reasonably priced model.
For ecommerce, apply by ordering tiered pricing, bundle tables, or comparison pages from highest price/quality down, and let customers click into mid- and entry-tier options from that anchor.
If you want to move a specific mid-tier item, place it immediately after the premium tier in the visual or copy order so the contrast works in its favor.
caveats: The Brunswick figures are one dealer's week-over-week results; your category and audience may respond differently.
Anchoring that feels manipulative, or pairing it with a first ask so extreme it seems bad-faith, can reduce trust and compliance.

cards.title: Small favors still get repaid — sometimes with much larger ones
cards.summary: The reciprocity obligation is uncomfortable enough that people often return more than they received, which is why small first favors can trigger large asks.
cards.use_when: Designing the size of a first free offer relative to the purchase or commitment you will later request.
steps: Start small but make the first favor real. In Regan's study, a 10-cent Coke led subjects to buy an average of two raffle tickets at 25 cents each (a 500% return on Joe's investment); some bought as many as seven.

Expect overshoot: because indebtedness is psychologically unpleasant and non-reciprocators are socially disliked, people may agree to a larger return than they received to clear the debt. Cialdini recounts a student who accepted a jump-start and a month later lent her nearly new car to the helper, who totaled it.

Apply in ecommerce by making the initial free gesture cheap for you but genuinely useful (a free sample, a small store credit, a helpful guide, free returns) and then asking for a specific next purchase or upgrade. The size mismatch can favor you.

Decide the size deliberately: the source warns that once you accept a gift you lose control of who you're indebted to, since the giver chooses the first favor and the return favor. As the seller, you control the first favor's size and form.
caveats: The coke-to-tickets ratio is a laboratory result, not a forecast for any store's conversion lift.
Unequal exchanges create resentment risk if the customer later feels cornered; keep the ask plausibly connected to the gift.

cards.title: Stockpile favors before you need them
cards.summary: Accumulated favors create a reservoir of obligation you can call in later, as LBJ did with Congress and Carter lacked.
cards.use_when: Planning long-horizon relationship building with suppliers, creators, affiliates, partners, or platforms before you need a specific ask.
steps: Provide favors and help to the other party well before making a request. The source contrasts Lyndon Johnson, who had many years of favors to legislators to call in and pushed a remarkable volume of legislation early, with Jimmy Carter, who campaigned as indebted to no one in Washington and found no one indebted to him when he needed votes.

For an ecommerce operator, the transferable move is to build goodwill with suppliers, fulfillment partners, influencers, and platform reps before a crunch — early payment or flexible terms, timely and accurate forecasts, giving an affiliate or creator extra exposure, helping a partner solve a problem — then drawing on that goodwill when you need rush production, better terms, a favor on inventory, or priority support.
Keep the ledger bilateral and non-transactional; the source frames the power as coming from unsolicited, stored goodwill rather than invoiced services.
This is a relationship-investment heuristic from political and anecdotal cases, not a measured ecommerce channel tactic.
caveats: Indebtedness is informal and fades; a favor given long ago may not translate into compliance today.
The Johnson/Carter comparison is the source's political analysis, not experimental evidence, and is vulnerable to confounds.

cards.title: Reciprocal concessions drive compromise and unequal returns
cards.summary: Reciprocating a concession — not just a favor — is the mechanism behind negotiation retreats, and it can produce returns far larger than the concession given.
cards.use_when: Structuring any multi-step offer, quote, or negotiation where you concede something first to invite a matching concession.
steps: Recognize the two sides of the rule: repay favors received, and make a concession to someone who has conceded to you. Cialdini's chocolate-bar episode shows the second: his shift from refusing tickets to buying candy mirrored the Scout's shift from a larger to a smaller request.

Use the first concession to induce the customer's concession. In the UCLA bargaining study cited, an opponent who opened with an extreme demand and then gradually retreated earned the most money, versus an opponent who held an extreme demand and one who held a moderate demand throughout.

Expect the retreating strategy to make the counterparty feel responsible for the outcome. Subjects facing the retreating opponent reported they had successfully influenced the opponent to take less, even though the opponent had been instructed to retreat no matter what. That felt responsibility is why people who say yes to a retreat-then-request sequence follow through and agree to further asks.

In ecommerce, apply this to quotes, custom orders, wholesale terms, or bundle ladders: make a visible, genuine concession step (larger pack, higher quantity, more premium service) before landing on the deal you intend, and note that the customer's felt ownership of the final terms can increase fulfillment and repeat agreement.

Follow-through evidence from the source: with rejection-then-retreat, 76% agreed to volunteer for two unpaid hours vs. 29% for a direct ask, and 85% of those showed up vs. 50% for the direct ask. In a blood-donation study, 84% of those in the retreat condition agreed to be called again later vs. 43% of those asked the single pint directly.
caveats: Concessions must be genuine in appearance; a transparent trick neutralizes the effect.
The follow-through percentages are from specific field experiments and should not be read as expected rates for any store.
Dislikes and extremes: if the opening ask is illegitimate, the retreat is not reciprocated — the source cites Bar-Ilan research on this.
